questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the agent loop?

options.text: To generate personality traits for the assistant
options.feedback: Wrong – personality is a separate concept, not the loop’s function.

options.text: To repeatedly call the LLM, run tools, and feed results back
options.feedback: Correct – the loop cycles LLM calls, tool execution, and prompt updates.

options.text: To store conversation history for later retrieval
options.feedback: Wrong – storing history is handled by session storage, not the loop itself.

options.text: To limit the number of tokens a model can generate
options.feedback: Wrong – token limits are a bound on the loop, not its core purpose.

questions.prompt: Why must the agent loop have a stopping condition?

options.text: To prevent infinite execution and ensure the agent eventually finishes
options.feedback: Correct – a clear stop condition avoids endless looping.

options.text: To allow the LLM to change its system prompt dynamically
options.feedback: Wrong – the system prompt is fixed for each run; the stop condition is unrelated.

options.text: To automatically log every tool execution for debugging
options.feedback: Wrong – logging is a separate practice, not the reason for a stop condition.

options.text: To enable the agent to switch between different LLM providers
options.feedback: Wrong – provider selection is done outside the loop, not by its stop condition.

questions.prompt: What role does logging each step of the loop serve?

options.text: It reduces the token usage of subsequent LLM calls

options.text: It lets failures be replayed and examined later

options.text: It automatically generates new tools for the agent

options.text: It determines how many iterations the loop should run
options.feedback: Wrong – iteration limits are set explicitly, not derived from logs.

questions.prompt: Why does placing static content first in a prompt improve caching?

options.text: The cache can match the unchanged tokens before the dynamic part
options.feedback: Correct – prefix matching stops at the first differing token, so static front matter stays cached.

options.text: Static content is smaller, so it fits in memory better
options.feedback: Incorrect – size isn’t the reason; ordering determines whether the cache can be reused.

options.text: Dynamic content is automatically compressed when placed later
options.feedback: Incorrect – compression isn’t part of prompt caching; ordering affects cache hits.

options.text: LLMs ignore tokens that appear after static content
options.feedback: Incorrect – LLMs process all tokens; they just don’t need to recompute cached KV pairs.

questions.prompt: When should you expect prompt caching to provide a net benefit?

options.text: Whenever the same exact user question is repeated
options.feedback: Incorrect – caching stores the KV pairs of the prompt prefix, not the final answer.

options.text: When the prompt prefix is at least about 1024 tokens
options.feedback: Correct – below that length the overhead outweighs savings, so caching is beneficial only after ~1024 tokens.

options.text: If the prompt contains any system instructions
options.feedback: Incorrect – system prompts can be cached, but they must be long enough to meet the token threshold.

options.text: Only when using a system that requires explicit cache flags
options.feedback: Incorrect – both automatic and explicit caching can work; the token length rule still applies.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended strategy when a rate‑limit error occurs?

options.text: Retry with exponential backoff
options.feedback: Correct – exponential backoff spreads retries over increasing intervals, helping respect rate limits.

options.text: Immediately resend the same request until it succeeds
options.feedback: Incorrect – sending requests without delay can worsen the rate‑limit problem.

options.text: Abort the operation and return an error to the user
options.feedback: Incorrect – the lesson advises queuing or shedding load, not hard failure.

options.text: Switch to output caching instead of retrying
options.feedback: Incorrect – output caching is unrelated to handling rate‑limit errors.

questions.prompt: How does increasing temperature affect the probability distribution?

options.text: It flattens the distribution, making low‑probability words more likely.
options.feedback: Correct – a higher temperature divides the logits by a larger number, reducing differences and flattening the softmax output.

options.text: It sharpens the distribution, favoring the highest‑probability word.
options.feedback: Wrong – sharpening occurs with lower temperature, not higher.

options.text: It removes the top‑K constraint from the sampling process.
options.feedback: Wrong – temperature does not affect top‑K; it only rescales probabilities.

options.text: It changes the model architecture to generate longer sentences.
options.feedback: Wrong – temperature is a sampling parameter, not a change to model architecture.

questions.prompt: When is top‑p (nucleus) sampling especially useful compared to top‑k?

options.text: When you want the candidate set size to adapt to the probability shape.
options.feedback: Correct – top‑p dynamically selects the smallest set whose cumulative probability exceeds p.

options.text: When you need a fixed number of tokens regardless of probabilities.
options.feedback: Wrong – that describes top‑k, not top‑p.

options.text: When you want to guarantee the highest‑probability token is always chosen.
options.feedback: Wrong – top‑p still samples randomly within the nucleus, not deterministic.

options.text: When you aim to eliminate any randomness from generation.
options.feedback: Wrong – top‑p introduces randomness; it does not remove it.

questions.prompt: Which setting is best for tasks like extraction or classification?

options.text: Low temperature (e.g., 0.5) to make outputs more deterministic.
options.feedback: Correct – lower temperature sharpens the distribution, favoring the most probable token for precise tasks.

options.text: High temperature (e.g., 2) to encourage creative wording.
options.feedback: Wrong – high temperature adds randomness, which can hurt accuracy in extraction.

options.text: A very large top‑k value to include many rare tokens.
options.feedback: Wrong – large top‑k may introduce irrelevant words, reducing precision.

options.text: A top‑p value of 0.1 to restrict the token set heavily.
options.feedback: Wrong – such a low p can overly limit options and still adds randomness, not ideal for deterministic tasks.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of a window function in SQL?

options.text: Combine rows into a single result

options.text: Order and number rows within a set

options.text: Create temporary tables for reuse

options.feedback: Filtering is done with WHERE, not with window functions.

questions.prompt: How does PARTITION BY affect the output of a window function?

options.text: It merges all rows into one group

options.text: It restarts numbering within each group

options.text: It removes duplicate rows from the result

options.text: COUNT()

questions.prompt: What is a primary benefit of using a server action in Next.js over a traditional API route for form submissions?

options.text: It requires a full page reload
options.feedback: A server action does not reload the page; it re-renders only needed server components.

options.text: It runs entirely on the client
options.feedback: Server actions run only on the server, not on the client.

options.text: It automatically updates UI without reloading the page
options.feedback: Server actions revalidate data and re-render components, updating the UI without a full reload.

options.text: It forces the use of useEffect for state updates
options.feedback: Server actions reduce the need for useEffect; they handle server-side logic directly.

questions.prompt: Which feature allows a server action to update data and then immediately refresh the relevant page content?

options.text: useTransition hook
options.feedback: useTransition is for client-side state changes; revalidation uses revalidatePath.

options.text: revalidatePath function
options.feedback: revalidatePath tells Next.js to revalidate the page after a mutation.

options.text: useOptimistic hook

options.text: The action property on a button
options.feedback: The action property triggers the server action; revalidation is separate.

questions.prompt: Why can server actions be defined outside of a server component and still be reused?

options.text: Because they cannot access fetched data
options.feedback: Outside functions can access data if passed; inside components they can close over fetched data.

options.text: Because the use server directive applies to all functions in a file
options.feedback: Placing 'use server' at the top of a file marks all exported functions as server actions.

options.text: Because they must be exported as default
options.feedback: They can be named exports; default export is not required.

options.text: Because they automatically become client components
options.feedback: Server actions remain server-side; they are not client components.

questions.prompt: Why do server components not increase the client bundle size?

options.text: Their code runs only on the server and isn’t sent to the client
options.feedback: Correct – server component code stays on the server, so the client receives only HTML.

options.text: They are automatically minified more than client components
options.feedback: Incorrect – minification isn’t the reason; the code simply never reaches the client.

options.text: Next.js strips out all imports from server components
options.feedback: Wrong – imports remain, but they execute on the server and aren’t bundled for the client.

options.text: Server components are compiled into CSS instead of JavaScript
options.feedback: Incorrect – they compile to HTML, not CSS, and still run as JavaScript on the server.

questions.prompt: What security benefit do server components provide?

options.text: Secret data and credentials never leave the server
options.feedback: Correct – because the component runs on the server, any secrets stay hidden from the client.

options.text: They encrypt the HTML sent to the browser
options.feedback: Incorrect – server components don’t encrypt HTML; they simply avoid sending secret code.

options.text: They disable all client‑side JavaScript by default
options.feedback: Wrong – client‑side JavaScript can still be used; server components just don’t add extra code.

options.text: They require a VPN connection for every request
options.feedback: Incorrect – no VPN is required; the security comes from keeping code server‑side.

questions.prompt: Why can server components be async functions?

options.text: They can await fetch or database calls directly on the server
options.feedback: Correct – server components run on the server, so they can use async/await without useEffect.

options.text: The client needs to handle the promise resolution
options.feedback: Incorrect – the promise resolves on the server before HTML is sent to the client.

options.text: Async functions reduce the size of the server bundle
options.feedback: Wrong – async nature doesn’t affect bundle size; it just simplifies data fetching.

options.text: They enable server‑side rendering of CSS modules
options.feedback: Incorrect – async functions relate to data fetching, not CSS handling.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of streaming in this context?

options.text: Display slow data instantly over the page shell
options.feedback: Correct. The lesson explains that streaming renders fast parts immediately while slow parts load.

options.text: Force all data to load before showing the shell
options.feedback: Wrong. Streaming prevents idle waiting; it does not make slow data appear before it is ready.

options.text: Hide the page shell until all data is ready
options.feedback: Wrong. The goal is to show the shell and fast content first, not hide them.

options.text: Block the entire page on the slowest request
options.feedback: Wrong. Streaming allows the shell to render while data fetches, not wait for a single request.

questions.prompt: How should you handle slow subtrees in Next.js 13?

options.text: Use it as a real fallback for slow subtrees
options.feedback: Correct. The lesson you should use Suspense with a real fallback for slow subtrees.

options.text: Wrap every component to ensure global consistency
options.feedback: Wrong. The fallback is for slow data, not for every internal app state.

options.text: Replace all server components to improve performance
options.feedback: Wrong. The lesson focuses on client-side UI updates, not replacing server components.

options.text: Mock network requests to speed up local development
options.feedback: Wrong. Suspense handles UI feedback for loading data, not mocking the network layer.

questions.prompt: What does adding a loading.tsx file accomplish for a route?

options.text: It streams the UI shell before data is ready
options.feedback: Correct. It lets the shell stream instantly while the server fetches data.

options.text: It prevents the first static render of the page
options.feedback: Wrong. The lesson states the initial static render is what might not cover all state.

options.text: It only adds a client-side visual loading indicator
options.feedback: Wrong. While it provides feedback, its primary function is server-side streaming of the shell.

options.text: It disables the built-in router cache for that route
options.feedback: Wrong. The loading file is independent of the router cache's functionality.

questions.prompt: Where should the "use client" directive be placed to keep bundle size small?

options.text: On every component file
options.feedback: Adding it everywhere makes many server components client-side, increasing bundle size.

options.text: At the boundary of a client subtree
options.feedback: Placing it at the tree's edge keeps only the leaf components client-side.

options.text: Only on pages that need interactivity
options.feedback: Marking an entire page client makes all its imports client-side, losing server benefits.

options.text: At the top of the layout file
options.feedback: The layout can stay server; putting it here would unnecessarily client‑load the whole app.

questions.prompt: What happens when a server component imports a component marked with "use client"?

options.text: The imported component stays server-side
options.feedback: A client directive forces the component and its imports to be client-side.

options.text: Only the imported component becomes client-side
options.feedback: The import triggers the client subtree, turning the component and anything below it client-side.

options.text: The import causes a runtime error
options.feedback: The import works; it just shifts the component to the client bundle.

options.text: The server component is recompiled to client-side
options.feedback: The parent component remains server; only the imported subtree changes.

questions.prompt: Why can importing a provider component into a client component still allow server children?

options.text: Because provider components are always server components
options.feedback: Provider components are typically client components, but they can pass children through.

options.text: The children pattern lets the provider wrap server components without making them client-side
options.feedback: By accepting children and rendering them, the provider can host server components inside a client tree.

options.text: Server components automatically become client when wrapped
options.feedback: Server components stay server unless imported into a client component.

options.text: The provider copies its context to the server
options.feedback: Context is only available in the client; server components don't receive it.

questions.prompt: What must you include when selecting a column together with an aggregate function?

options.text: A GROUP BY clause containing the non‑aggregate column
options.feedback: Correct – the non‑aggregate column must be listed in GROUP BY.

options.text: A HAVING clause referencing the aggregate function
options.feedback: HAVING filters after grouping; it does not satisfy the requirement for non‑aggregate columns.

options.text: A DISTINCT keyword on the SELECT list
options.feedback: DISTINCT removes duplicates but does not replace GROUP BY for mixed columns.

options.text: An ORDER BY clause on the aggregate result
options.feedback: ORDER BY only sorts the output; it does not address grouping rules.

questions.prompt: Which clause can filter rows based on an aggregate value?

options.text: HAVING
options.feedback: Correct – HAVING applies conditions to aggregated results.

options.text: WHERE
options.feedback: WHERE cannot reference aggregate functions; it filters before grouping.

options.text: GROUP BY
options.feedback: GROUP BY defines how rows are grouped, not how they are filtered.

options.text: SELECT
options.feedback: SELECT lists columns; it does not perform filtering on aggregates.

questions.prompt: If you add a city column to the SELECT list, what must change in the query?

options.text: Add city to the GROUP BY clause
options.feedback: Correct – every non‑aggregated column must appear in GROUP BY.

options.text: Move city to the HAVING clause
options.feedback: HAVING filters on aggregates, not on plain column inclusion.

options.text: Replace COUNT with SUM for city
options.feedback: SUM is an aggregate function; it does not resolve the grouping error.

options.text: Add a WHERE condition on city
options.feedback: A WHERE clause can filter rows but does not satisfy the GROUP BY requirement.

questions.prompt: What does a foreign key primarily enforce in a database?

options.text: It guarantees column values are unique
options.feedback: Uniqueness is enforced by unique constraints, not foreign keys.

options.text: It links two tables by reference
options.feedback: Correct. A foreign key references a primary key to link tables.

options.text: It automatically deletes related rows
options.feedback: That is a delete behavior choice, not a primary function of foreign keys.

options.text: It stores the row’s ID in both tables
options.feedback: IDs are stored in primary keys, not by foreign keys.

questions.prompt: Which is a requirement for a column to be referenced by a foreign key?

options.text: It must contain only nulls
options.feedback: Nulls would break referential integrity.

options.text: It must have unique values
options.feedback: The referenced column must be unique (often a primary key).

options.text: It must be indexed automatically
options.feedback: Indexes help performance but are not a requirement for a foreign key.

options.text: It must be a numeric type
options.feedback: Any data type that matches the referenced column can be used.

questions.prompt: Choosing delete behavior for a foreign key affects what?

options.text: The speed of query execution
options.feedback: Delete behavior is about referential integrity, not query speed.

options.text: Which rows can be removed when a parent row is deleted
options.feedback: It determines if child rows are deleted, set null, or prevent deletion.

options.text: The format of the primary key
options.feedback: Primary key format is unrelated to delete behavior.

options.text: The presence of unique constraints on the child table
options.feedback: Unique constraints are independent of delete behavior.

questions.prompt: When should you choose a native PostgreSQL type over JSONB?

options.text: For data that has a fixed structure like timestamps
options.feedback: Correct – precise types preserve constraints and performance.

options.text: When the data will never be queried
options.feedback: Wrong – even unqueried data benefits from appropriate types for storage.

options.text: If you need to store binary files
options.feedback: Incorrect – binary files use BYTEA, not JSONB.

options.text: Whenever you want flexibility for future changes
options.feedback: Misleading – flexibility is a JSONB reason, but fixed data should stay typed.

questions.prompt: Which JSONB operator extracts a top‑level key’s value?

options.feedback: Right – -> returns the value of the specified key.
No – #> navigates a path of keys, not a single top‑level key.
Incorrect – @> checks containment, not extraction.
Wrong – ~> is not a JSONB operator in PostgreSQL.

questions.prompt: When you must search inside a JSONB column, what is the recommended practice?

options.text: Create a GIN index on the JSONB column
options.feedback: Correct – a GIN index speeds containment and key/value queries.

options.text: Store the same data in a separate text column
options.feedback: Wrong – duplicating data adds overhead without improving JSONB queries.

options.text: Always cast JSONB to text for comparison
options.feedback: Incorrect – casting loses index use and is slower.

options.text: Rely on sequential scans because JSONB is small
options.feedback: Misleading – even small JSONB benefits from proper indexing when queried.

questions.prompt: When reading an EXPLAIN plan, which part of the tree should you start with?

options.text: Innermost node
options.feedback: You begin at the innermost node and work outward to understand the plan flow.

options.text: Outermost node
options.feedback: The outermost node is the last to be processed, not the starting point.

options.text: Middle node
options.feedback: There is no single 'middle'; plans are hierarchical.

options.text: The first line of the output
options.feedback: The first line is just a label; the real plan starts deeper in the tree.

questions.prompt: A sequential scan in PostgreSQL is most likely to occur when?

options.text: A column is filtered by a WHERE clause
options.feedback: A WHERE clause often triggers an index scan if an index exists.

options.text: There is no suitable index for the query
options.feedback: Without an index, PostgreSQL must read the whole table— a sequential scan.

options.text: The query uses an ORDER BY on an indexed column
options.feedback: Indexed ORDER BYs use index scans; sequential scans still happen if no index.

options.text: The table contains fewer than 100 rows
options.feedback: Row count alone does not force a sequential scan; indexes still matter.

questions.prompt: Why is a large difference between estimated and actual row counts in an EXPLAIN plan a concern?

options.text: It shows the database is running too many queries
options.feedback: The issue is about estimation accuracy, not query volume.

options.text: It indicates statistics may be stale or inaccurate
options.feedback: Big gaps mean statistics mislead PostgreSQL, leading to poor plans.

options.text: It means the query is returning more data than expected
options.feedback: The estimate vs actual gap is about prediction, not data volume.

options.text: It reflects that the query is using too much memory
options.feedback: Memory usage is unrelated to estimate/actual row count differences.

questions.prompt: What is the primary advantage of using pg_dumpall over pg_dump?

options.text: Includes cluster-wide configuration and rules
options.feedback: Correct. The transcript explains that pg_dump all includes information about cluster configuration and rules.

options.text: Limiting backup to one specific database
options.feedback: Incorrect. pg_dump is explicitly for backing up a single database, not the whole cluster.

options.text: Copying physical files from disk
options.feedback: Incorrect. pg_basebackup is the tool described for file-system level backups.

options.text: Setting up a replication standby
options.feedback: Incorrect. The lesson does not mention pg_dump all creating a replica database.

questions.prompt: What characterizes a logical backup in this lesson?

options.text: Generating SQL scripts to recreate objects
options.feedback: Correct. The speaker defines logical backups as generating SQL files with commands to recreate objects.

options.text: Copying raw physical files from disk
options.feedback: Incorrect. Copying physical files is the definition of a physical backup.

options.text: Instantiating a separate server process
options.feedback: Incorrect. Creating a second server instance is not the definition provided.

options.text: Scheduling automated job executions
options.feedback: Incorrect. The lesson describes creating backups, not scheduling job execution.

questions.prompt: Why is a connection pooler recommended in front of the database?

options.text: Preventing idle sessions from exhausting capacity
options.feedback: Correct. The notes state that pooling stops idle connections from exhausting the server.

options.text: Enforcing strong password policies
options.feedback: Incorrect. Enforcing strong passwords is not the stated purpose of pooling.

options.text: Monitoring and logging slow queries
options.feedback: Incorrect. Monitoring slow queries is not mentioned as a pooler function.

options.text: Encrypting data during transmission
options.feedback: Incorrect. Encrypting data in transit is not the function described for the pooler.

questions.prompt: Why does a B‑tree index improve search speed compared to a linked‑list table?

options.text: It reduces search complexity from linear to logarithmic time
options.feedback: Correct – B‑tree traversal visits far fewer nodes, giving O(log n) instead of O(n).

options.text: It stores all rows in memory for instant lookup
options.feedback: Wrong – B‑trees are stored on disk; they improve speed by structure, not by keeping everything in memory.

options.text: It eliminates the need for any disk I/O during queries
options.feedback: Wrong – Disk I/O still occurs; pages are read, but fewer pages are needed.

options.text: It guarantees constant‑time lookup for any column value
options.feedback: Wrong – Lookup is logarithmic, not constant; performance still grows with data size.

questions.prompt: When is an index on a Boolean column usually not helpful?

options.text: Because it creates two large, nearly equal branches that must both be scanned
options.feedback: Correct – With only two distinct values, each branch can be large, offering little pruning.

options.text: Because PostgreSQL does not support indexes on Boolean types
options.feedback: Wrong – PostgreSQL can index Booleans, but the index may not improve performance.

options.text: Because the index would have to store the whole row for each value
options.feedback: Wrong – Indexes store pointers, not full rows; the issue is low selectivity, not size.

options.text: Because B‑tree indexes cannot be built on columns with only two distinct values
options.feedback: Wrong – B‑trees can be built on any column; they just may not be efficient for low‑cardinality data.

questions.prompt: What trade‑off must be considered when adding any index?

options.text: Every insert incurs extra work to keep the index balanced
options.feedback: Correct – Adding rows requires updating and possibly splitting pages, increasing write cost.

options.text: Indexes automatically compress data, reducing storage space
options.feedback: Wrong – Indexes occupy additional space; they do not compress the underlying table.

options.text: Indexes eliminate the need for query planning by the optimizer
options.feedback: Wrong – The planner still decides whether to use an index; it does not bypass planning.

options.text: Adding an index always speeds up both reads and writes equally
options.feedback: Wrong – Writes become slower due to index maintenance, even though reads may be faster.

questions.prompt: Which pattern lets you change a schema while both old and new code run simultaneously?

options.text: Add then drop
options.feedback: This simple add-drop does not allow simultaneous old and new code.

options.text: Expand, migrate, contract
options.feedback: Expand, migrate, contract lets you modify the schema with both versions running.

options.text: Drop then add
options.feedback: Dropping first blocks writes and stops old code from running.

options.text: Rename then recompile
options.feedback: Renaming alone doesn't keep old and new code in sync.

questions.prompt: What is a common cause of long locks during a schema change?

options.text: Adding a NOT NULL column without default
options.feedback: That operation is quick and does not lock the table.

options.text: Changing a column type from int4 to int8
options.feedback: Changing a type requires a table rewrite and locks the table.

options.text: Creating a unique index concurrently
options.feedback: Concurrent unique index creation avoids long exclusive locks.

options.text: Adding a column with a default value
options.feedback: That also locks the table for a rewrite, but the key example given was type change.

questions.prompt: Why should migrations be reversible or explicitly forward‑only?

options.text: To allow rolling back during development
options.feedback: Reversible migrations let you undo changes if needed.

options.text: Because forward‑only saves disk space
options.feedback: Disk space is unrelated to migration direction.

options.text: Reversible migrations speed up deployment
options.feedback: They help recovery, not necessarily deployment speed.

options.text: Forward‑only migrations are required by Postgres
options.feedback: Postgres accepts both reversible and forward‑only migrations.

questions.prompt: What is the primary goal of normalizing a database?

options.text: To eliminate duplicated data and update anomalies
options.feedback: Correct. The primary purpose of normalization is organizing data to remove duplication and update anomalies, ensuring each table focuses on one thing.

options.text: To increase the total storage size of the database
options.feedback: Incorrect. While it involves restructuring, the goal is not to increase storage size but to ensure data integrity by removing redundancy.

options.text: To make every write operation happen in a single step
options.feedback: Incorrect. Normalization focuses on logical data structure, not the physical speed of writes, though it can impact performance indirectly.

options.text: To merge multiple tables into one large comprehensive table
options.feedback: Incorrect. Normalization splits tables into smaller ones focusing on one entity, not combining them into larger, more complex tables.

questions.prompt: Which type of dependency must be removed to reach second normal form?

options.text: Partial dependencies on composite keys
options.feedback: Correct. In 2NF, every non-key column must depend on the entire primary key. If they depend on just part of it, it is a partial dependency.

options.text: Transitive dependencies between independent columns
options.feedback: Incorrect. Transitive dependencies relate to 3NF, where non-key columns depend on other non-key columns rather than the primary key.

options.text: Columns containing multiple indivisible values
options.feedback: Incorrect. Multiple values in a single column violate atomicity, which is the requirement for First Normal Form, not Second Normal Form.

options.text: Any intentional duplication of data for read speed
options.feedback: Incorrect. Denormalization is a deliberate choice to trade safety for read speed, not a violation of normal form rules.

questions.prompt: What specific dependency type is eliminated in third normal form?

options.text: Non-key columns depend directly on the primary key
options.feedback: Correct. Transitive dependencies occur when non-key columns depend on other non-key columns instead of directly on the primary key, which 3NF eliminates.

options.text: Composite keys are used by no other columns
options.feedback: Incorrect. A composite key being ignored by all columns is not the standard definition of a transitive dependency described in the lesson.

options.text: Read speed is prioritized over data safety
options.feedback: Incorrect. Denormalization is described as a justified trade-off for read speed, not a violation of third normal form rules.

options.text: Single columns store multiple indivisible values
options.feedback: Incorrect. Storing multiple values in one column violates First Normal Form (atomicity), not Third Normal Form.

questions.prompt: What is the primary benefit of rewriting predicates before adding an index?

options.text: It allows the existing index to be used efficiently
options.feedback: Correct – rewriting predicates can make the condition match the index, avoiding a function on the indexed column.

options.text: It automatically creates a new index for the query
options.feedback: Wrong – rewriting does not create indexes; it makes the query compatible with existing indexes.

options.text: It reduces the need for prepared statements
options.feedback: Wrong – predicate rewriting is unrelated to prepared statements; it deals with how the optimizer can use indexes.

options.text: It eliminates the need to verify the query plan later
options.feedback: Wrong – even after rewriting, you should still verify the plan to ensure the index is being used.

questions.prompt: Why should row count be reduced as early as possible in a query plan?

options.text: It minimizes work for later operators like joins or aggregates
options.feedback: Correct – filtering early cuts the number of rows processed by subsequent steps, improving overall performance.

options.text: It forces PostgreSQL to use a sequential scan
options.feedback: Wrong – reducing rows early does not force a sequential scan; it can enable index scans instead.

options.text: It guarantees the query will run in constant time
options.feedback: Wrong – early row reduction helps speed the query but does not make execution time constant.

options.text: It allows the database to skip the EXPLAIN ANALYZE step
options.feedback: Wrong – you still need to verify the plan; early filtering does not remove the need for analysis.

questions.prompt: What does “verify the improvement with a fresh plan” mean in practice?

options.text: Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE after changes to see the new execution strategy
options.feedback: Correct – a fresh EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows whether the rewrite or index is actually being used.

options.text: Check the query’s runtime without looking at the execution plan
options.feedback: Wrong – timing alone doesn’t confirm that the optimizer chose the intended plan.

options.text: Restart the PostgreSQL server to apply the changes
options.feedback: Wrong – a server restart isn’t required; a new plan is generated per execution.

options.text: Delete and recreate the index to ensure it’s up to date
options.feedback: Wrong – verification is about the plan, not about rebuilding the index.

questions.prompt: Which join returns only rows with matching keys in both tables?

options.text: INNER JOIN
options.feedback: Inner joins keep only matching rows from both tables.

options.text: LEFT JOIN
options.feedback: Left joins include all left table rows, even if no match.

options.text: RIGHT JOIN
options.feedback: Right joins include all right table rows, regardless of matches.

options.text: FULL JOIN
options.feedback: Full joins return all rows from both tables, matching where possible.

questions.prompt: What happens to a row in the left table when a LEFT JOIN finds no matching right table row?

options.text: The row is excluded from results
options.feedback: A LEFT JOIN keeps the row; it just shows NULLs for right table columns.

options.text: The row is included with NULLs for right columns
options.feedback: Without a match, the left row remains, right columns are NULL.

options.text: The row is duplicated for each unmatched right row
options.feedback: Duplication occurs only when there are multiple matches, not when none.

options.text: The row triggers an error
options.feedback: SQL does not error; it simply returns the left row with NULLs.

questions.prompt: Where should a condition that only applies to the joined table be placed to avoid accidental fan-out?

options.text: In the WHERE clause
options.feedback: A WHERE filter applies after the join, potentially filtering joined rows.

options.text: In the ON clause
options.feedback: Placing the condition in ON limits rows during the join, preventing fan-out.

options.text: In the SELECT list
options.feedback: SELECT list cannot filter rows; it only determines output columns.

options.text: In a subquery
options.feedback: A subquery is another method but not the recommended approach in this context.

questions.prompt: What does authentication verify in a web application?

options.text: The user's identity
options.feedback: Correct – authentication checks who the user claims to be.

options.text: What pages the user can view
options.feedback: Wrong – that is the role of authorization, not authentication.

options.text: The server's configuration settings
options.feedback: Wrong – authentication does not involve server settings.

options.text: How data is encrypted in transit
options.feedback: Wrong – encryption is a separate security measure, not authentication.

questions.prompt: Why must authorization be enforced on the server each request?

options.text: Server‑side checks prevent client tampering
options.feedback: Correct – only the server can reliably enforce permissions for every request.

options.text: It speeds up page loading times
options.feedback: Wrong – enforcing authorization does not primarily affect performance.

options.text: It replaces the need for authentication
options.feedback: Wrong – authorization works after authentication; both are required.

options.text: It stores user passwords securely
options.feedback: Wrong – password storage is part of authentication, not authorization.

questions.prompt: An insecure direct object reference is best prevented by:

options.text: Checking user permissions for each object on the server
options.feedback: Correct – verifying authorization for every object blocks IDOR attacks.

options.text: Hiding object IDs in the URL
options.feedback: Wrong – obscuring IDs does not stop unauthorized access if checks are missing.

options.text: Using stronger passwords for authentication
options.feedback: Wrong – password strength does not address direct object reference issues.

options.text: Encrypting all traffic with TLS
options.feedback: Wrong – TLS protects data in transit but does not enforce object‑level permissions.

questions.prompt: Which XSS type stores malicious code on the server so every user sees it on page load?

options.text: Stored XSS
options.feedback: Correct. Stored XSS persists in the database and runs for all users.

options.text: Reflected XSS
options.feedback: Wrong. Reflected XSS only runs when the malicious URL is visited.

options.text: DOM-based XSS
options.feedback: Wrong. DOM-based XSS manipulates the page in the browser, not stored server‑side.

options.text: CSRF
options.feedback: Wrong. CSRF is a different attack that tricks a user into submitting a request.

questions.prompt: What is the primary reason for using contextual output encoding?

options.text: To escape characters for the exact output context
options.feedback: Correct. Contextual encoding prevents injected scripts from executing.

options.text: To block all user input
options.feedback: Wrong. Encoding does not remove input but neutralizes dangerous characters.

options.text: To replace scripts with harmless text
options.feedback: Wrong. Encoding keeps the data but changes its meaning only in the right context.

options.text: To sanitize the database entries
options.feedback: Wrong. Encoding is applied at output time, not database storage.

questions.prompt: Which header is used to limit where a page’s JavaScript can load from?

options.text: Content Security Policy (CSP)
options.feedback: Correct. CSP lets you specify allowed script sources and block others.

options.text: X-Frame-Options
options.feedback: Wrong. X-Frame-Options controls framing, not script sources.

options.text: Strict-Transport-Security
options.feedback: Wrong. HSTS forces HTTPS, not script loading restrictions.

options.text: Referrer-Policy
options.feedback: Wrong. Referrer-Policy controls the Referer header, not script sources.

questions.prompt: Why does a CSRF attack succeed even when cookies are marked Secure and HttpOnly?

options.text: The browser automatically includes those cookies with cross-site requests
options.feedback: Correct – Secure and HttpOnly only protect cookie access, they are still sent automatically with any request to the origin.

options.text: Secure cookies can be read by JavaScript on other sites
options.feedback: Wrong – HttpOnly prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie, even on other sites.

options.text: HttpOnly cookies block all cross‑origin form submissions
options.feedback: Wrong – HttpOnly does not affect whether a form can be submitted; it only restricts script access.

options.text: Secure attribute encrypts the cookie value for each request
options.feedback: Wrong – Secure only requires transmission over HTTPS; it does not encrypt the value per request.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of setting SameSite on cookies?

options.text: Prevent the browser from sending the cookie on cross‑site requests
